I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over forty years. The North China Plain doesn't give you many choices — our soils, our rainfall, our markets all point the same direction: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots. That's what I'll do again this year.

I have about 20 mu of cultivated land. All of it goes into this rotation. I'm 67 now — I can't do heavy manual labor the way I used to, so I hire a small team for harvesting, but I make every input decision myself.

**Wheat (already in ground since October, now entering jointing):** I planted improved wheat — Jimai 22 — because I've had good results with it and it suits our soil. For the spring top-dressing I'll apply urea at jointing, moderate nitrogen, not excessive. I've seen too many neighbors burn their yield potential by over-fertilizing and then over-irrigating to compensate. We have groundwater depletion problems here — the people from China Agricultural University drilled that into us years ago and they were right. I'll irrigate at jointing and again at heading. That's two irrigations. Maybe a third if we get a dry spell before grain filling, but I'll watch the sky first.

For pests and disease: one fungicide pass at heading for powdery mildew and scab, and one aphid spray if thresholds are reached. That's two applications total if needed.

**Maize (to be planted June after wheat harvest):** I'll go straight into no-tillage direct seeding into wheat stubble — saves time, saves fuel, and conserves moisture. I use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, which I've trusted for years. Maize gets less water from me than wheat because summer rains usually handle it. One irrigation to establish if June is dry, possibly one more at tasseling. Fertilizer: a controlled-release compound applied at planting, then a top-dress at the 10-leaf stage.

I expect about 480 kg/mu from wheat and 600 kg/mu from maize if weather cooperates. At 67, I'm not trying to push record yields. I want stable output, low risk, and sustainable water use.
